genes/0.notes: Biallelic AHCY missense or truncating variants cause the disease. The index genotype includes p.Trp112Ter and p.Tyr143Cys; the review shorthand T112stop is not a p.Thr112Ter allele. Recombinant p.Arg49Cys and p.Asp86Gly have condition-dependent functional defects. Homozygous p.Arg49His recurs in Pakistani families with mild childhood presentations, but one confirmed adult developed HCC; a uniformly benign outcome or measured residual activity for this allele is not established. The 2024 report cites allele frequencies of approximately 0.000065 in South Asia and 0.000012 globally, not carrier frequencies or disease prevalence. ClinGen classified the gene-disease association as Definitive in December 2024; the older Moderate wording remaining in its narrative was superseded by that reevaluation.

evidence.snippet: acute onset of 1 or more of the 8 major groups of manifestations: psychosis, memory deficit, speech disturbance, seizures, movement disorder, loss of consciousness, autonomic dysfunction, and central hypoventilation
evidence.explanation: Speech disturbance is included among the major clinical manifestation groups used for anti-NMDAR encephalitis case inclusion in this cohort.

evidence.snippet: Most affected were memory (mean -0.67 ± 0.89 SD, p = 0.25) and language (-0.75 ± 1.06 SD, p = 0.23).

evidence.snippet: some patients with rapidly progressive psychiatric symptoms or cognitive impairment, seizures, abnormal movements, or coma of unknown cause, had an autoimmune disease.

evidence.snippet: We reported that 48.4% of patients displayed autonomic symptoms, and other studies on anti-NMDAR encephalitis also reported elevated incidences of autonomic dysfunction (Titulaer: 37%–48%; Dalmau: 69%).
evidence.explanation: The Western China cohort reports autonomic symptoms in nearly half of patients, placing the phenotype in the FREQUENT frequency band.

evidence.snippet: movement disorder (p = 0.001), central hypoventilation (p < 0.001), elevated CSF white blood cell count (p < 0.001), elevated CSF protein level (p = 0.027), and abnormal MRI (p = 0.002) were associated with 1-year functional status in univariate analysis.
evidence.explanation: Central hypoventilation is identified as a clinically important feature associated with functional outcome.

evidence.snippet: Tumours, usually ovarian teratoma, and herpes simplex encephalitis are known triggers of NMDAR autoimmunity.

edges/0.description: Triggered autoreactive B-cell responses feed local CNS/CSF anti-NMDAR antibody production.

evidence.snippet: Patients’ antibodies labelled nearly all clusters of NMDA receptors (figure 4).
evidence.explanation: Patient antibodies directly bind postsynaptic NMDAR clusters, linking intrathecal antibodies to receptor-cluster effects.

edges/1.description: Locally produced antibodies bind extracellular NR1/GluN1 epitopes on neuronal NMDA receptors.

evidence.snippet: Together, these findings show that patients’ antibodies produce a selective and reversible decrease of NMDA-receptor clusters in postsynaptic dendrites.

edges/2.description: Reduced surface and postsynaptic NMDAR availability impairs NMDAR-dependent synaptic signaling.

evidence.snippet: autoantibodies serve as a diagnostic marker and alter NMDAR-related synaptic transmission.

edges/3.description: NMDAR hypofunction maps to the characteristic encephalitis syndrome of psychiatric symptoms, seizures, movement disorder, coma, autonomic dysfunction, and hypoventilation.

evidence.snippet: The blood-brain barrier (BBB), which separates the brain from the peripheral circulatory system, is crucial for antibodies and immune cells to enter or exit the CNS.

edges/4.description: Barrier dysfunction may facilitate antibody and immune-cell traffic that sustains the intrathecal immune compartment.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical manifestations of the anti-NMDAR encephalitis were psychosis (182, 82.7%) and seizures (178, 80.9%).

edges/5.description: Psychotic symptoms are the most frequently reported manifestation of the encephalitic syndrome and are usually what brings patients to attention.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical manifestations of the anti-NMDAR encephalitis were psychosis (182, 82.7%) and seizures (178, 80.9%).

edges/6.description: Seizures arise from the same encephalitic network dysfunction and are co-dominant with psychosis in large cohorts.

evidence.snippet: After immunotherapy, all cases showed a complete recovery from catatonic signs.
evidence.explanation: Removing the antibody-driven disease process abolishes the catatonia, which supports this node as its source; the inference step is the treatment-reversal argument rather than a direct mechanistic measurement.

edges/7.description: The catatonic syndrome is produced by this encephalitic state rather than by a comorbid primary psychiatric illness. evidence.snippet: After multivariate analysis, the clinical hallmarks of ANMDARE consisted of a catatonia-delirium comorbidity, tonic-clonic seizures, and orolingual dyskinesia.

edges/8.description: Orolingual and limb dyskinesias are among the multivariate-selected hallmarks of the syndrome, and are more frequent in children.

edges/9.description: Cognitive impairment, with memory among the most affected domains, is part of the syndrome and can persist after the acute illness resolves.

evidence.snippet: Herein, patients with HSE-NMDARE have a poorer long-term prognosis than patients with regular NMDARE.

evidence.snippet: This study provides the first evidence that geographic and climatic factors including latitude, mean annual temperature, and ultraviolet exposure, might modify disease risk.

evidence.snippet: We studied a large sample of male children from birth to adulthood to determine why some children who are maltreated grow up to develop antisocial behavior, whereas others do not.
evidence.explanation: Establishes childhood maltreatment as the exposure under study in a prospective birth-to-adulthood cohort of antisocial outcomes.

evidence.snippet: rs9806493 is an eQTL for SLCO3A1 (Solute Carrier Organic Anion Transporter Family Member 3A1), a ubiquitously expressed gene with strong expression in brain regions that include the anterior cingulate and frontal cortices.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the gene implicated by the genome-wide significant ASPD association and its regional brain expression.

evidence.snippet: Polygenic risk score analysis identified positive correlations between ASPD and smoking, ADHD, depression traits, and posttraumatic stress disorder.
evidence.explanation: Supports the shared, non-specific character of ASPD genetic risk.

steps/1.description: Genome-wide association analysis of ASPD diagnostic criteria in 3217 alcohol-dependent participants identified a chromosome 15 variant, rs9806493, an eQTL for SLCO3A1, a gene strongly expressed in anterior cingulate and frontal cortices. Polygenic risk for ASPD correlates positively with smoking, ADHD, depression traits and PTSD, indicating substantially shared rather than disorder-specific genetic risk.

evidence.snippet: A functional polymorphism in the gene encoding the neurotransmitter-metabolizing enzyme monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) was found to moderate the effect of maltreatment.
evidence.explanation: Prospective birth cohort establishes MAOA genotype as a moderator of the maltreatment effect.

steps/2.description: A functional polymorphism in MAOA, encoding the monoamine-metabolizing enzyme monoamine oxidase A, moderates the effect of childhood maltreatment on later antisocial outcomes. Maltreated boys with the high-activity genotype were less likely to develop antisocial problems, so the genotype acts as a moderator of environmental sensitivity rather than as an independent cause.

evidence.snippet: AABS was defined as meeting all ASPD criteria except CD before age 15.
evidence.explanation: The survey defines the adult-only antisocial syndrome as ASPD minus the conduct-disorder-before-15 criterion, establishing that criterion as required for the ASPD diagnosis.

steps/3.description: A childhood pattern of aggression, destruction, deceit and serious rule violation with onset before age 15. This node is not merely a risk factor but a diagnostic requirement: DSM-5 does not permit an ASPD diagnosis without it, which is what makes ASPD a developmental rather than an adult onset condition.

steps/4.description: The adult clinical syndrome: a pervasive and persistent pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, expressed as aggression, deceit, impulsivity, irresponsibility and absence of remorse.

evidence.snippet: ASPD is characterized by a pattern of irresponsible, impulsive, aggressive, and remorseless behaviors beginning by early adolescence and persisting into adulthood.
evidence.explanation: The NESARC-III review names aggressive behavior as a core feature of ASPD.

steps/5.description: Irritability and aggressiveness, including repeated physical fights or assaults, is a core DSM-5 criterion.

evidence.snippet: Polygenic risk score analysis identified positive correlations between ASPD and smoking, ADHD, depression traits, and posttraumatic stress disorder.
evidence.explanation: The shared polygenic signal with ADHD supports an impulsivity dimension in ASPD only through an inference step from genetic correlation to phenotype, so it is graded indirect.

steps/6.description: Impulsivity or failure to plan ahead is a DSM-5 criterion and is shared with the ADHD phenotypes that ASPD polygenic risk correlates with.

evidence.snippet: One in 4 US adults exhibits syndromal antisocial behavior, with similar sociodemographic and psychiatric correlates and disability regardless of whether onset occurred before 15 years of age, illustrating the clinical and public health significance of both ASPD and AABS.

steps/7.description: The defining pervasive disregard for and violation of the rights of others, including deceitfulness and absence of remorse.

Because childhood conduct disorder is a diagnostic prerequisite for ASPD, prevention at this stage acts upstream of the adult disorder.

evidence.snippet: We have identified specific missense substitutions involving adjacent amino acids (Ser252Trp and Pro253Arg) in the linker between the second and third extracellular immunoglobulin (Ig) domains of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) in all 40 unrelated cases of Apert syndrome studied.
evidence.explanation: Original identification of S252W and P253R mutations in FGFR2 linker region in all 40 Apert syndrome cases, establishing causative role of these mutations.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate loss of ligand specificity of FGFR2 with retained ligand dependence for receptor activation.
evidence.explanation: This directly constrains the activating mechanism: Apert FGFR2 variants broaden ligand recognition but do not make receptor activation ligand independent.

steps/1.description: Apert syndrome is caused almost exclusively by the adjacent FGFR2 S252W and P253R substitutions in the linker between immunoglobulin-like domains II and III, defining a recurrent activating receptor genotype.

evidence.snippet: These structures demonstrate that both mutations introduce additional interactions between FGFR2 and FGF2, thereby augmenting FGFR2-FGF2 affinity.
evidence.explanation: Structural analysis directly shows that the recurrent Apert mutations increase FGFR2 ligand affinity.

evidence.snippet: Alterations in FGFR2 ligand affinity and specificity may allow inappropriate autocrine or paracrine activation of FGFR2.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports altered ligand specificity as the receptor-level mechanism that drives aberrant FGFR2 activation in Apert syndrome.

steps/2.description: The S252W and P253R FGFR2 mutations create gain-of-function receptor states with increased FGF affinity and altered ligand specificity, enabling inappropriate autocrine or paracrine receptor activation.

evidence.snippet: FGF2 secretion was greater.
evidence.explanation: Apert P253R osteoblasts show increased FGF2 output, supporting a reinforcing autocrine signaling loop.

evidence.snippet: All together these findings suggest increased constitutive receptor activity in Apert mutant osteoblasts and an autocrine loop involving the FGF2 pathway in modulation of Apert osteoblast behavior.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports a constitutively active FGFR2/FGF2 autocrine signaling node.

steps/3.description: Apert-mutant osteoblast-lineage cells show increased constitutive receptor activity together with an FGF2-driven autocrine loop that reinforces aberrant FGFR2 signaling.

evidence.snippet: WT and MT FGFR2 induced ERK1/2 but not JNK or PI3K/AKT phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: This shows that activated FGFR2 engages the ERK1/2 cascade in the Apert model.

steps/4.description: Apert-mutant FGFR2 activates the ERK1/2 cascade in mesenchymal cells as one branch of the downstream signaling response.

evidence.snippet: MT, but not WT, also increased protein kinase C (PKC) activity.
evidence.explanation: This shows mutant-specific activation of the PKCalpha signaling branch.

steps/5.description: The Apert-mutant receptor engages a mutant-specific PKCalpha signaling branch that amplifies the osteogenic program beyond wild-type FGFR2 signaling.

evidence.snippet: Both WT and MT FGFR2 increased early and late osteoblast gene expression and matrix mineralization.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports enhanced osteogenic differentiation and mineralization in the Apert FGFR2 model.

steps/6.description: Activated Apert FGFR2 signaling accelerates osteoblast differentiation and matrix mineralization within cranial suture tissues.

evidence.snippet: In Ap mice, the coronal suture (CS) was fused prematurely at P1.
evidence.explanation: The Apert mouse model directly supports premature coronal suture fusion as a tissue-level mechanistic event.

steps/7.description: Excess osteogenic activity in coronal suture mesenchyme causes early closure of the coronal sutures and distorts cranial growth.

evidence.snippet: Abnormalities associated with Apert syndrome include premature fusion of coronal sutures system (coronal sutures and less frequently lambdoid suture) resulting in brachiturricephalic dismorphism and impaired skull base growth.
evidence.explanation: This supports impaired skull-base growth as a distinct downstream consequence of Apert craniosynostosis.

steps/8.description: Premature cranial suture closure restricts skull-base growth and contributes to the characteristic craniofacial growth pattern of Apert syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The airway compromise seen in patients with Apert syndrome is attributable more to the pharyngeal region than to the nasal cavity, with a gradually worsening trend from the anterior to the posterior airway, resulting in a significantly reduced volume in the hypopharynx.
evidence.explanation: CT-based comparison supports an anatomically localized pharyngeal restriction node.

steps/9.description: Reduced pharyngeal dimensions and other multilevel anatomic restrictions produce clinically important upper-airway obstruction in Apert syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Almost all patients had otitis media with effusion (glue ear), which tended to persist into adult life. More than 56 per cent of cases developed permanent conductive hearing loss by 10-20 years.
evidence.explanation: A 70-record cohort directly supports persistent effusion and later conductive loss, while not proving a single upstream anatomic mechanism.

steps/10.description: Persistent middle-ear effusion is nearly universal in a large historical Apert cohort and commonly progresses to permanent conductive hearing impairment; the precise intervening craniofacial anatomy is not resolved in the curated evidence.

evidence.snippet: Speech, language, communicative participation, and hearing difficulties are pervasive in patients with AS. The severity and functional impact of these difficulties are magnified in patients with the S252W mutation.
evidence.explanation: The genotype-confirmed cohort supports a linked craniofacial, hearing, and speech burden but does not isolate palate as the sole cause of speech difficulty.

steps/11.description: FGFR2-related craniofacial development can include cleft palate, which contributes with hearing and structural factors to pervasive speech-sound difficulty.

evidence.snippet: The main CNS abnormalities were prominent convolutional markings (67 %), ventriculomegaly (48 %), crowded foramen magnum (36 %), deficient septum pellucidum (13 %), and corpus callosum agenesis in 11 %.
evidence.explanation: Imaging of 94 patients supports the frequency of CNS structural findings without establishing their mechanism or functional impact.

steps/12.description: Nonprogressive ventricular enlargement occurs frequently, but its developmental mechanism and clinical significance remain largely unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Major C-spine findings were present in 50.8 % of patients and included fusion of posterior elements of C5/C6 (50 %) and C3/4 (27 %). Multilevel fusion was seen in 20 %.
evidence.explanation: The imaging cohort directly supports cervical vertebral fusion as a frequent structural feature.

steps/13.description: Progressive skeletal synostosis in Apert syndrome commonly involves posterior cervical vertebral elements and may span multiple levels.

evidence.snippet: Apert syndrome (AS) is characterized by craniosynostosis, midfacial hypoplasia, and bony syndactyly. It is an autosomal dominantly inherited disease caused by point mutations (S252W or P253R) in fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) 2. genes/0.notes: No causal gene has been cloned for DFNA47 despite the locus having been mapped by linkage analysis in 2003 (multipoint LOD 4.26; a critical interval of approximately 9 cM flanked by markers D9S268 and D9S942, with peak two-point LOD 3.67 at marker D9S162). MYO1A, a cochlear-expressed unconventional myosin gene reported in 2003 to carry multiple mutations in Italian hearing-loss patients, is NOT the DFNA47 gene: MYO1A maps to the separate DFNA48 locus (15q22-q25), and its proposed association with nonsyndromic deafness has itself since been refuted by an independent genotypic-ascertainment study that found no bilateral moderate-or-greater sensorineural hearing loss among carriers of the implicated MYO1A variants. This entry should not be bound to MYO1A. A separate recessive locus, DFNB83, was mapped to 9p23-p21.2 in a consanguineous Palestinian family and overlaps the DFNA47 cytogenetic band; whether the two represent allelic disorders of one still-uncloned gene is an unconfirmed hypothesis based only on the two loci's proximity, not a demonstrated fact -- no shared causal variant has been published for either locus.

steps/1.description: BLOC1S1 encodes a shared subunit of the BLOC-1 and BORC complexes. Disease-causing variants impair this shared module, with current evidence indicating a BORC-predominant neurologic disorder rather than the full canonical BLOC-1/Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome phenotype. Mild pigmentary findings can occur, but bleeding diathesis, pulmonary fibrosis, granulomatous colitis, and immunodeficiency should not be generalized to BLOC1S1-related disease from other BLOC-1 subunit disorders.

steps/1.description: Activating TEK variants are present in affected tissues, often at low mosaic allele fractions. Identical variants across sampled lesions support a shared mutant lineage; the developmental timing and precise founding cell cannot be reconstructed from sequencing alone.

evidence.snippet: ... both cause ligand-independent activation of TIE2, and increase survival, invasion, and colony formation when expressed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells.

steps/1.description: GDF5 (CDMP1) is a secreted BMP-family ligand that acts through BMPR1B to drive chondrocyte differentiation and joint formation. BDC alleles are heterozygous frameshift, nonsense, and active-domain missense variants. Truncating alleles simply remove a functional copy; the missense alleles reach the same endpoint by a different route, failing to form the disulfide-linked dimers that the mature growth factor requires. Both converge on functional haploinsufficiency — roughly half the normal GDF5 activity — which distinguishes BDC from the dominant-negative BMPR1B alleles of type A2 and from the processing-site GDF5 allele that also causes A2.

evidence.snippet: GDF5, the most prominent member of the GDFs, was shown to play a vital role in the differentiation of chondrocytes and the formation of joints
evidence.explanation: Establishes GDF5's dual role in chondrocyte differentiation and joint formation.

evidence.snippet: BDC is characterized by brachymesophalangia of the second, third, and fifth fingers, sometimes together with hyperphalangia, usually of the second and third fingers.
evidence.explanation: Describes the paired shortening-plus-extra-segment pattern that the segmentation defect produces.

evidence.snippet: As a consequence of the close interactions within the network, overlapping phenotypes are generated that are, nevertheless, characterized by specific recognizable patterns.
evidence.explanation: Supports the reading that the distinct brachydactyly patterns arise from graded perturbations of one shared regulatory network.

steps/2.description: GDF5 is expressed in the joint interzone and controls both chondrocyte differentiation in the digital ray and the segmentation that separates phalanges. Lowering it disturbs the segmentation program in two directions at once, which is why BDC uniquely pairs missing middle-phalangeal length with supernumerary phalangeal segments: some interzones fail to make a normal segment, while others produce an extra, malformed one. GDF5 is also the BDA2 and (in semidominant families) the BDA1 gene, so the type of brachydactyly tracks the allele's specific effect on ligand maturation and receptor affinity rather than the identity of the gene.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The four published homozygotes do not agree. Two had reduced spontaneous cytotoxicity with severe viral disease. A third had recurrent viral infection and a difficult course after BCG, Epstein-Barr and varicella zoster, yet formal testing showed normal spontaneous cytotoxicity and normal ADCC, and that report explicitly asked whether the genotype is causally related to NK deficiency. A fourth, found on newborn screening, is clinically well with normal NK lytic function and normal CD56-bright / CD56-dim distribution; her lymphopenia was traced to a 22q11.2 deletion.
Population data are the strongest argument against simple causation: the allele sits near 5% frequency overall, with roughly a hundred homozygotes in gnomAD. A fully penetrant recessive immunodeficiency allele cannot be that common. The 2021 report concludes the variant is unlikely to be a direct genetic cause and proposes low-penetrance risk instead.
Ascertainment is the obvious confounder in both directions: the affected patients were found because they were ill, and the well homozygote was found because of an unrelated screen. What would settle it is a systematic NK-function study of unselected homozygotes, which nobody has published. Until then this entry records the mechanism that was measured in affected patients without asserting that the genotype produces it in everyone.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Three mechanisms are in play and they should not be collapsed.
First, a genuine artifact. Because L66H abolishes the B73.1 epitope, a panel that gates NK cells as CD3-negative, CD56-positive AND CD16-positive scores an L66H homozygote as having almost no NK cells, while the same blood gated on CD3-negative, CD56-positive gives a normal count. That is exactly what happened in the newborn-screening case: under one gate NK cells were absent, under another they were 26%. The 1996 report predicted this, warning that combining CD16 and CD56 antibodies on the same fluorochrome would leave these homozygotes undiagnosed.
Second, and importantly, this does not explain the index patient. Jawahar gated on CD56-positive, CD3-negative cells without CD16, so the reduced count reported there is not the artifact and remains unexplained. Treating the artifact as a blanket dismissal would be wrong.
Third, the second and fourth patients had normal NK numbers outright.
The practical consequence is that NK lymphopenia is not usable as a screening criterion for this entity, and that any reported NK count for an L66H homozygote has to be read together with the gating strategy that produced it.

open_questions/2.rationale:
The step from a measurable in vitro cytotoxicity deficit to severe, persistent EBV, VZV and HPV disease in vivo is asserted on plausibility and on the known role of NK cells in herpesvirus control, not demonstrated. No reported patient has had NK-specific reconstitution, there is no animal model of the L66H allele, and the quantitative contribution of this pathway to viral control in humans is unmeasured.
The two homozygotes added in review widen this gap rather than narrowing it, and in opposite directions. One had a severe viral course - recurrent respiratory infection, a difficult course after BCG vaccination, and severe problems with Epstein-Barr and varicella zoster - while his spontaneous cytotoxicity and ADCC were both normal, so a comparable clinical picture arose without the mechanism this entry proposes. The other has the genotype, normal cytotoxicity, and no disease at all. Any account of how the cytotoxicity defect produces the infection phenotype now has to explain both.

genes/4.notes: X-linked IRS4 variants were reported in two brothers with isolated central hypothyroidism and an unaffected carrier mother. MONDO files the IRS4 form as hypothyroidism, congenital, nongoitrous, 9 (MONDO:0026732), which this entry now carries as a subtype row.

evidence.snippet: Newborn screening (NBS) for congenital hypothyroidism (CH) was started in 1979 in Japan, and early diagnosis and treatment improved the intelligence prognosis of CH patients.
evidence.explanation: This guideline abstract supports early treatment for congenital hypothyroidism generally; the specific levothyroxine management details are inferred from standard endocrine care rather than directly stated in the abstract.

treatments/0.description: Thyroid hormone replacement is the core treatment after diagnosis. In possible MPHD, clinicians must also consider adrenal insufficiency before or during thyroid hormone replacement.

evidence.snippet: Newborn screening (NBS) for congenital hypothyroidism (CH) was started in 1979 in Japan, and early diagnosis and treatment improved the intelligence prognosis of CH patients.
evidence.explanation: This supports early treatment benefit for congenital hypothyroidism generally, while the specific levothyroxine mechanism is standard endocrine inference from thyroid hormone replacement.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Levothyroxine replacement bypasses deficient endogenous thyroid hormone generation by supplying thyroid hormone pharmacologically.

evidence.snippet: To date, central CH is the only pituitary hormone deficiency suitable for newborn screening (NBS), providing an opportunity for early detection of MPHD.
evidence.explanation: This supports newborn screening as a clinically relevant detection strategy for central congenital hypothyroidism and associated MPHD.

evidence.snippet: In the Netherlands, we have a unique T4-TSH-thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) NBS algorithm for CH, which enables the detection of primary and central CH.
evidence.explanation: This supports a concrete T4-TSH-TBG screening implementation.

treatments/1.description: T4-inclusive newborn screening with reflex TSH and TBG is a secondary prevention strategy that can detect central congenital hypothyroidism early.

evidence.snippet: For the first time, we demonstrate a correlation between the altered IGHMBP2 biochemical activity associated with the D565N and H924Y mutations and disease severity and pathology in patients and our Ighmbp2 mouse models.
evidence.explanation: Residual activity determines severity along the SMARD1-CMT2S continuum.

evidence.snippet: In the context of the compound heterozygous patient, we demonstrate that the total biochemical activity associated with IGHMBP2-D565N and IGHMBP2-H924Y proteins is improved over IGHMBP2-D565N alone.
evidence.explanation: Summed activity of two alleles explains compound heterozygous phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: The discovery that IGHMBP2 functions as an RNA/DNA helicase was an important step, but it did not reveal the pathogenic mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Review framing of the helicase function and the open mechanism question.

steps/1.description: CMT2S alleles reduce, but do not abolish, IGHMBP2 abundance and its ATP-dependent DNA/RNA helicase activity. Association with the activator ABT1 stimulates IGHMBP2 ATPase and helicase activity, and CMT2S variants such as p.His924Tyr retain ABT1 association and substantial activity, whereas SMARD1 variants such as p.Asp565Asn lose it; in compound heterozygotes the summed activity of the two mutant proteins predicts severity. This residual-activity threshold is the disorder-specific insult to peripheral neurons.

evidence.snippet: We provide a mechanism proposing that ABT1 decreases disease pathology in FVB-Ighmbp2nmd/nmd mutants by optimizing IGHMBP2 biochemical activity (ATPase and helicase activity). Our studies provide insight into SMARD1 pathogenesis, suggesting that ABT1 modifies IGHMBP2 activity as a means to regulate pre-rRNA processing.
evidence.explanation: Proposes pre-rRNA processing as the affected pathway.

evidence.snippet: IGHMBP2 appears to be a multifunctional factor involved in several cellular processes that regulate gene expression. It is difficult to determine which processes, when dysregulated, lead to pathology.
evidence.explanation: Records the unresolved link between RNA functions and pathology.

evidence.snippet: we found that IGHMBP2 deletion modestly reduces global translation
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of reduced global translation in IGHMBP2-knockout cells, supporting the DECREASED translation modifier.

evidence.snippet: We generated ATF4 reporter cell lines and found IGHMBP2 knockout cells demonstrate basal, chronic ISR activation.
evidence.explanation: Source for the low-grade integrated stress response in knockout cells.

steps/2.description: IGHMBP2, with ABT1, binds the 47S pre-rRNA 5' external transcribed spacer and U3 snoRNA, implicating it in pre-rRNA processing; it is also associated with tRNA and translation machinery. Loss of activity is proposed to impair ribosome biogenesis and translation, with a low-grade integrated stress response in knockout cells, but which of IGHMBP2's RNA-metabolic roles drives neuronal pathology is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypic characterization of the homozygous models found progressive peripheral motor and sensory axonal degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration of axonal degeneration in CMT2S models.

evidence.snippet: All patients had a predominantly axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with subsequent muscle atrophy, but without obvious sensory symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Human electrophysiological and clinical correlate.

steps/3.description: Long peripheral motor and sensory axons degenerate progressively, producing an axonal neuropathy with reduced amplitudes and largely preserved conduction velocities; CMT2S knock-in mice show progressive motor and sensory axonal degeneration in femoral nerves with motor deficits and mechanical allodynia. In contrast to SMARD1, spinal alpha-motor neurons supplying the diaphragm are relatively spared.

evidence.snippet: There was decreased limb skeletal muscle fiber area and increased neuromuscular junction (NMJ) denervation in Ighmbp2D564N/H922Y mice.
evidence.explanation: NMJ denervation and muscle atrophy in the compound heterozygous model.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with CMT2S, Ighmbp2H922Y/H922Y mice did not have altered lifespans nor respiratory pathology.
evidence.explanation: The CMT2S-like allele spares respiration and lifespan.

evidence.snippet: Neuromuscular junction analyses revealed high fatigue and chaotic tetanus formulation in untreated patient cells. We demonstrate rescue of NMJ function following ASO treatment, captured by a reduction in fatigue and chaotic tetanus responses.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived NMJ dysfunction and its rescue by IGHMBP2 restoration.

steps/4.description: Loss of motor axons denervates neuromuscular junctions, causing neurogenic distal muscle atrophy, weakness, foot deformity and gait impairment. In compound heterozygous Ighmbp2 D564N/H922Y mice NMJ denervation and reduced fibre area are marked, whereas the CMT2S-like H922Y homozygote shows minimal NMJ changes even at six months; patient-derived neuromuscular co-cultures show high fatigue and chaotic tetanus that are rescued by restoring IGHMBP2.

evidence.snippet: All patients had a predominantly axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with subsequent muscle atrophy, but without obvious sensory symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Defining neuropathy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Three patients presented with childhood-onset axonal predominant sensorimotor polyneuropathies, whereas the other case was diagnosed with SMARD1
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort confirming the axonal sensorimotor phenotype.

steps/5.description: Predominantly axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy with reduced compound muscle and sensory action potential amplitudes and relatively preserved conduction velocities.

evidence.explanation: Initial symptom frequencies across 45 patients. The frequency band is inferred from the share presenting with this feature, which is a lower bound on its lifetime frequency.

steps/6.description: Muscle weakness, usually of the lower limbs first, is the commonest initial symptom and spreads proximally over time.

evidence.snippet: All patients had a predominantly axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with subsequent muscle atrophy, but without obvious sensory symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Muscle atrophy secondary to the neuropathy.

evidence.explanation: Frequency of delayed milestones as the initial symptom.

steps/8.description: Delayed motor milestones are the presenting feature in a fifth of patients with infantile onset.

evidence.explanation: Foot drop as an initial symptom. The frequency band is inferred from the share presenting with this feature, which is a lower bound on its lifetime frequency.

steps/10.description: Foot drop from weakness of the anterior compartment muscles.

evidence.snippet: A 9 month old boy presented with bilateral feet deformities and axonal neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Foot deformity as the presenting feature.

evidence.explanation: Sensorimotor involvement with subclinical sensory symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Two patients had signs of autonomic neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Autonomic involvement in the original series.

steps/13.description: Signs of autonomic neuropathy in a minority of patients.

evidence.snippet: At 9 years, he developed diaphragmatic weakness, following which he was established on non-invasive ventilation.
evidence.explanation: Documented late diaphragmatic involvement.

steps/14.description: Late-onset diaphragmatic weakness requiring non-invasive ventilation is reported in otherwise typical CMT2S; infantile diaphragmatic paralysis defines SMARD1 instead.

evidence.snippet: The IGHMBP2/ABT1 complex interacts with the 47S pre-rRNA 5' external transcribed spacer and U3 small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA), suggesting that the IGHMBP2/ABT1 complex is important for pre-rRNA processing.
evidence.explanation: Links helicase function to pre-rRNA processing.

evidence.snippet: Further sequencing revealed a total of 11 CMT2 families with recessively inherited IGHMBP2 gene mutations.
evidence.explanation: The paper that established IGHMBP2 as the CMT2S gene, in 11 recessive families.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in CMT2 were predicted to be less aggressive as compared to those in SMARD1, and fibroblast and lymphoblast studies indicate that the IGHMBP2 protein levels are significantly higher in CMT2 than SMARD1, but lower than controls, suggesting that the clinical phenotype differences are related to the IGHMBP2 protein levels.
evidence.explanation: Residual protein level as the basis of the CMT2S-versus-SMARD1 distinction.

evidence.snippet: We report on 5 patients with neuropathy from 3 families who carried truncating mutations in IGHMBP2. Contrary to the "classic" phenotype, they did not manifest with respiratory distress, but with progressive sensorimotor neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes IGHMBP2 as a cause of axonal neuropathy without respiratory distress.

evidence.snippet: One third of identified mutations represented presumed loss-of-function variants (nonsense, frameshift and splicing), while two-thirds were missense changes which clustered in the helicase and ATPase domains.
evidence.explanation: Variant spectrum.

evidence.snippet: However, clinical phenotypes differed markedly as the elder with sensorimotor axonal neuropathy had still unaffected respiratory function at 4.5 years, whereas the younger presented as infantile spinal muscular atrophy and died from relentless respiratory failure at 11 months.
evidence.explanation: Intrafamilial SMARD1/CMT2S discordance with identical genotype.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic IGHMBP2 (11q13.3) variants cause CMT2S; the same gene causes SMARD1, and compound heterozygotes for one severe and one milder allele can present with either phenotype, even within a sibship. Two-thirds of reported CMT2S variants are missense changes clustering in the helicase and ATPase domains and one-third are presumed loss-of-function (nonsense, frameshift, splice) alleles; missense changes near the RNA-binding channel or the nucleotide-binding pocket may be associated with more severe outcomes. Residual protein level and biochemical (ATPase/helicase) activity correlate with the SMARD1-versus-CMT2S outcome. Deep intronic variants activating cryptic splice sites are a recognised class.

treatments/0.description: Care is supportive and extrapolated from general CMT practice: individualised physiotherapy, occupational therapy, ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids, pain management, and orthopaedic correction of fixed foot deformity or scoliosis after specialist assessment.

evidence.snippet: At 9 years, he developed diaphragmatic weakness, following which he was established on non-invasive ventilation. Our case emphasizes the importance of life long respiratory surveillance for patients with CMT2S and expands the phenotype of this condition.
evidence.explanation: Basis for surveillance and ventilatory support.

treatments/1.description: Lifelong respiratory surveillance is advised because diaphragmatic weakness can appear years after onset; non-invasive ventilation is instituted when it does.

evidence.snippet: Corroborating previous findings, both constructs effectively rescued the pathological phenotype, significantly improving survival, body weight, and motor function while preserving motor neurons and neuromuscular junctions.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical efficacy in the IGHMBP2-deficient mouse.

evidence.snippet: Open-label, single intrathecal injection study of a AAV9 vector carrying the IGHMBP2 gene for IGHMBP2-related diseases.
evidence.explanation: Registered trial covering IGHMBP2-related diseases including CMT2S.

treatments/2.description: Single intrathecal AAV9-IGHMBP2 delivery is in a phase I/IIa trial enrolling genetically confirmed SMARD1 or CMT2S (NCT05152823). In the SMARD1 mouse, optimised AAV9-IGHMBP2 vectors rescued survival, motor function, motor neurons and neuromuscular junctions and resolved spinal cord inflammatory changes, with a truncated MeCP2 (P546) promoter giving superior long-term efficacy and safety.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Restores IGHMBP2 expression in motor neurons irrespective of genotype.

evidence.snippet: ASO treatment of patient fibroblasts significantly increased the ratio of restored wild-type transcript to cryptic exon-containing transcript and resulted in over a 50% increase in IGHMBP2 protein levels.
evidence.explanation: Molecular rescue in patient cells.

treatments/3.description: For a compound heterozygous patient with a deep intronic cryptic-splice variant, a 19-mer antisense oligonucleotide blocking the cryptic acceptor restored wild-type transcript, raised IGHMBP2 protein by over 50% in fibroblasts, rescued neuromuscular junction function in vitro and was well tolerated intrathecally in rats; an N-of-1 strategy applicable only to that variant class.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Blocks a variant-created cryptic splice site so that normally spliced, stable IGHMBP2 transcript is restored.

evidence.snippet: Intracerebroventricular injection of scAAV9-Abt1 decreases FVB-Ighmbp2nmd/nmd disease pathology, significantly increases lifespan, and substantially decreases neuromuscular junction denervation.
evidence.explanation: Preclinical proof of the modifier approach.

treatments/4.description: Intracerebroventricular scAAV9-Abt1 reduced disease pathology, extended lifespan and decreased neuromuscular junction denervation in the SMARD1-nmd mouse by stimulating the ATPase and helicase activity of residual IGHMBP2; a modifier-based strategy potentially suited to hypomorphic CMT2S alleles.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Increases the activity of residual mutant IGHMBP2 through its activator ABT1.

evidence.snippet: The clinical presentation in Patients 1 and 3 were consistent with SMARD1, whereas Patients 2 and 4 were in agreement with CMT2S.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates the intrafamilial phenotypic range relevant to counselling.

treatments/5.description: Autosomal recessive counselling with a 25% recurrence risk; the SMARD1-CMT2S continuum within a sibship should be explained.

evidence.snippet: More than 20 years after the link between IGHMBP2 and SMARD1 was revealed, and 10 years after the discovery of the association between IGHMBP2 and CMT2S, the pathogenic mechanism of these diseases is still not well defined.
evidence.explanation: Review statement of the mechanistic gap.

open_questions/0.rationale: IGHMBP2 has several proposed roles in gene expression and the field has not determined which, when dysregulated, causes neurodegeneration; the residual-activity threshold that separates CMT2S from SMARD1 is established at the biochemical level but its cellular basis in neuron subtypes is not.

evidence.snippet: Here, we examined chickenpox and shingles notifications from Thailand and found strong seasonal incidence in both diseases, with a 3-month lag between peak chickenpox transmission season and peak shingles reactivation.
evidence.explanation: Time-series analysis demonstrates robust seasonal structure in chickenpox transmission.

evidence.snippet: We established significant seasonality of varicella notifications
evidence.explanation: Independent surveillance analysis confirms statistically significant varicella seasonality.

evidence.snippet: In immunocompromised patients with altered cell mediated immunity, and rarely in healthy individuals, varicella results in a life-threatening infection.
evidence.explanation: Review establishing that altered cell-mediated immunity is the primary risk factor for severe varicella.

evidence.snippet: Infection with varicella zoster virus (VZV) causes varicella (chickenpox), which can be severe in immunocompromised individuals, infants and adults.
evidence.explanation: VZV primer confirming increased severity in immunocompromised individuals.

evidence.snippet: Varicella Outbreak Among Recent Arrivals to New York City, 2022-2024.
evidence.explanation: MMWR report documenting a varicella outbreak in congregate shelter settings among recent arrivals, demonstrating the role of overcrowding in transmission.

evidence.snippet: Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) is a pathogenic human alpha herpes virus that causes varicella (chicken pox) as a primary infection and, following a variable period of latency in different ganglionic neurons, it reactivates to produce herpes zoster (shingles).
evidence.explanation: Review establishing VZV's primary infection route and lifecycle.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) involves a cell-associated viremia during which infectious virus is carried from sites of respiratory mucosal inoculation to the skin.
evidence.explanation: Study directly establishing the respiratory mucosal inoculation site as the origin of VZV pathogenesis in the SCID-hu xenograft model.

steps/3.description: VZV enters the host through the upper respiratory tract via inhalation of infectious aerosols or direct contact with vesicle fluid. The virus initially replicates in the nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue (including tonsils) and regional lymph nodes, infecting CD4+ T lymphocytes with activation/memory and skin-homing features that serve as vehicles for subsequent systemic dissemination.

evidence.snippet: VZV DNA, primarily in T-lymphocytes, is detected as early as 8-10 days prior to rash and can persist for a week.
evidence.explanation: Key study demonstrating T-lymphocyte-associated VZV viremia preceding the rash.

evidence.snippet: VZV sEVs are non-infectious yet transcriptionally altered primary human cells, suppressing the antiviral type 1 interferon response and promoting neuroinvasion of a secondary pathogen in vivo.
evidence.explanation: Study demonstrating VZV immune evasion through suppression of type I interferon responses via extracellular vesicles.

evidence.snippet: ORF61 down-modulates the IRF3-mediated IFN-β pathway by degradation of activated IRF3 via direct interaction, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of VZV infection.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic study demonstrating that VZV ORF61 protein degrades activated IRF3 via ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, directly supporting the IRF3 antagonism described in the viremia entry.

evidence.snippet: During viremia the virus preferentially infected memory T-cells, initially central memory T-cells and subsequently effector memory T-cells.
evidence.explanation: Simian varicella virus study in non-human primates demonstrating preferential memory T-cell infection during viremia, providing in vivo evidence for VZV T-cell tropism during systemic dissemination.

steps/4.description: Following initial replication in lymphoid tissue, VZV disseminates via cell-associated viremia in T lymphocytes. VZV DNA is detectable in T-lymphocytes as early as 8-10 days prior to rash onset. The secondary viremia seeds the virus to the skin and mucous membranes, producing the characteristic vesicular exanthem. Concurrent innate immune evasion through IRF3 antagonism (by ORF61p, ORF47p, and IE-62) and suppression of type I interferon signaling facilitates systemic spread.

evidence.snippet: we report a virus-mediated immune-evasion strategy that disarms MAIT cell responses.
evidence.explanation: Study showing VZV disrupts MAIT cell polyfunctional effector responses, which are important at barrier sites like skin, supporting the mechanism of cutaneous immune evasion during vesicle formation.

evidence.snippet: HLA-DR and ICAM-1 expressions were not observed in VZV- and HSV-infected keratinocytes, contrasting with their upregulation in the surrounding epidermis and inside nonviral blisters.
evidence.explanation: Immunohistochemistry study of human herpes zoster (not primary varicella) lesions demonstrating MHC-II and ICAM-1 downregulation in VZV-infected keratinocytes. Since the same virus infects the same cell type, these immune evasion mechanisms are biologically relevant to primary varicella cutaneous pathology as well.

evidence.snippet: VZV gE inhibited MAVS oligomerization and STING translocation to disrupt MAVS- and STING-mediated interferon (IFN) responses, and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy was required for VZV gE-mediated inhibition of IFN production.
evidence.explanation: Study demonstrating that VZV glycoprotein E promotes mitophagy to evade innate antiviral signaling, tested in a 3D human skin organ culture model, directly relevant to immune evasion during cutaneous infection.

steps/5.description: VZV infects epidermal keratinocytes, causing ballooning degeneration, multinucleated giant cell formation, and intraepidermal vesiculation. Viral envelope glycoproteins (gB/gE, gH/gL) promote cell-to-cell fusion and syncytium formation, supporting spread through skin without requiring extracellular virion release. The characteristic rash progresses through macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts, with lesions in multiple stages simultaneously (centripetal distribution).

evidence.snippet: we discover numerous VZV latency-associated transcripts (VLTs)-like circRNAs (circVLTslytic), which contain multiple exons and different isoforms within the same back-splicing breakpoint.
evidence.explanation: Study characterizing VLT-related transcripts and their roles during VZV infection, supporting the latency transcription model.

evidence.snippet: following a variable period of latency in different ganglionic neurons, it reactivates to produce herpes zoster (shingles).
evidence.explanation: Review confirming lifelong ganglionic latency with subsequent reactivation as herpes zoster.

evidence.snippet: It is now established beyond doubt that latent VZV is predominantly located in human ganglionic neurons. Virus gene transcription during latency is epigenetically regulated, and appears to be restricted to expression of at least six genes, with expression of gene 63 being the hallmark of latency.
evidence.explanation: Authoritative review on VZV ganglionic latency establishing neuronal localization and the epigenetically regulated, restricted transcription program dominated by gene 63.

steps/6.description: During primary infection, VZV gains access to peripheral nerves and sensory ganglia, establishing lifelong latency in cranial nerve and dorsal root ganglia neurons. Latency is characterized by highly restricted viral transcription dominated by VZV latency-associated transcripts (VLTs) and VLT-ORF63 fusion transcripts, while most lytic genes are silenced. The virus may reactivate decades later as herpes zoster, particularly with aging or immunosuppression.

evidence.snippet: Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) is a pathogenic human alpha herpes virus that causes varicella (chicken pox) as a primary infection
evidence.explanation: Review confirming vesicular exanthem as the defining clinical feature of primary VZV infection (chickenpox).

evidence.snippet: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) can be detected in the blood from approximately 5 days before to 4 days after varicella.
evidence.explanation: Study establishing temporal relationship between viremia and the characteristic varicella rash.

steps/7.description: Generalized pruritic vesicular rash with centripetal distribution, typically appearing first on the trunk and spreading to the face and extremities. Lesions appear in successive crops over 3-5 days, with simultaneous presence of macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts.

evidence.snippet: It is a common childhood illness characterised by an itchy vesicular rash and fever, which usually resolves spontaneously without medical intervention.
evidence.explanation: Clinical review explicitly identifying fever as a characteristic feature of childhood chickenpox.

evidence.snippet: The rash typically starts on the chest, back, and face and then spreads, accompanied by fever, fatigue, pharyngitis, and headaches, usually lasting 5 to 7 days.
evidence.explanation: StatPearls reference documenting fever as a core accompanying symptom of the varicella rash lasting 5-7 days.

steps/8.description: Low-grade to moderate fever typically precedes or accompanies the rash onset, usually lasting 3-5 days. Fever reflects the systemic viremia and immune activation during acute infection.

evidence.snippet: It is a common childhood illness characterised by an itchy vesicular rash and fever
evidence.explanation: Clinical review explicitly identifying pruritus (itchy rash) as a characteristic feature of childhood chickenpox.

evidence.snippet: Chickenpox results in a skin rash forming small, itchy blisters that scab over
evidence.explanation: StatPearls reference confirming itchy blisters as the hallmark presentation of chickenpox.

steps/9.description: Intense itching of the vesicular lesions is a hallmark symptom and a major source of morbidity, particularly in children.

evidence.snippet: Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) is a pathogenic human alpha herpes virus that causes varicella (chicken pox) as a primary infection
evidence.explanation: Review documenting varicella as a systemic infection with constitutional symptoms including malaise.

steps/10.description: General feeling of discomfort, fatigue, and reduced appetite commonly accompanies the acute phase of infection.

evidence.snippet: VZV DNA, primarily in T-lymphocytes, is detected as early as 8-10 days prior to rash and can persist for a week.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that VZV viremia is T-lymphocyte-associated, detected before rash onset.

edges/0.description: Infected tonsillar T cells enter the bloodstream, producing cell-associated viremia.

evidence.snippet: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) can be detected in the blood from approximately 5 days before to 4 days after varicella.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the temporal relationship between viremia and rash onset.

edges/1.description: Viremia seeds VZV to skin where glycoprotein-mediated cell-to-cell spread produces vesicular lesions.

evidence.snippet: following a variable period of latency in different ganglionic neurons, it reactivates to produce herpes zoster (shingles).
evidence.explanation: Confirms that VZV establishes ganglionic latency during primary infection.

edges/2.description: During viremia, VZV also gains access to peripheral nerves and sensory ganglia.

edges/3.description: Primary systemic VZV infection commonly produces fever.

edges/4.description: Primary systemic VZV infection commonly produces constitutional malaise.

edges/5.description: Epidermal VZV spread produces the characteristic vesicular exanthem.

edges/6.description: VZV vesicles are characteristically itchy.

evidence.snippet: Here, we examined chickenpox and shingles notifications from Thailand and found strong seasonal incidence in both diseases, with a 3-month lag between peak chickenpox transmission season and peak shingles reactivation.
evidence.explanation: Time-series analysis of national notifications showing strong seasonal structure in chickenpox incidence. It establishes that transmission varies by season without identifying which seasonal factor does the work.

edges/7.description: Transmission rises and falls with the calendar rather than moving in one direction, which is why this is recorded as modulating rather than predisposing. What drives the cycle, whether school terms, humidity, or ultraviolet exposure, is not established, so the intervening steps are left unknown.

evidence.snippet: In immunocompromised patients with altered cell mediated immunity, and rarely in healthy individuals, varicella results in a life-threatening infection.
evidence.explanation: States that altered cell-mediated immunity turns varicella into a life-threatening infection, which is the containment failure this link records at the viremia node.

edges/8.description: Cell-mediated immunity is what normally contains the T-cell-associated viremia, so losing it lets dissemination run further and reach viscera. Recorded as exacerbating rather than triggering because the exposure does not start the infection; it removes the brake on a stage already under way.

evidence.snippet: Secondary attack rate (SAR) was lower in hepatitis A (43.3%) than those for varicella (75.0%) and mumps (65.3%)
evidence.explanation: Prospective household-contact study putting the varicella secondary attack rate at 75 percent, the highest of the three infections compared. It quantifies close contact rather than crowding as such.

edges/9.description: More susceptible people per infectious case gives the airborne virus more chances to reach a new respiratory mucosa. The measured setting is the household, the best quantified close-contact arrangement; crowding beyond the household is inferred from it, which is why the link is graded partial.

evidence.snippet: As HZ is preventable by vaccination, national HZ vaccination recommendations should include the need for and timing of vaccination
evidence.explanation: Review confirming vaccination as the primary prevention strategy for VZV disease, applicable to both varicella and herpes zoster.

treatments/0.description: Live attenuated varicella vaccine (Oka strain) is the primary preventive measure. Two-dose childhood vaccination achieves greater than 90% effectiveness against any disease and nearly 100% against severe disease.

evidence.snippet: The duration and magnitude of VZV DNAemia correlates with immune status and the efficacy of antiviral therapy.
evidence.explanation: Study demonstrating that antiviral therapy modulates VZV viremia, supporting acyclovir as standard treatment.

treatments/1.description: Oral acyclovir is recommended for adolescents, adults, and immunocompromised patients. Intravenous acyclovir is used for severe disease or immunocompromised hosts. Treatment is most effective when initiated within 24 hours of rash onset.

evidence.snippet: debilitating symptoms including neuropathic pain, and complications such as post-herpetic neuralgia, vision loss, and rarely, stroke, and increased severity in immunocompromised individuals.
evidence.explanation: Review documenting the symptomatic burden of VZV disease that necessitates supportive care.

treatments/2.description: Symptomatic management includes antipyretics (avoiding aspirin due to Reye syndrome risk), antihistamines for pruritus, and calamine lotion. Good hygiene prevents bacterial superinfection of lesions.

evidence.snippet: Guanylate cyclase C (GUCY2C) is a tumor-suppressing receptor silenced by loss of expression of its luminocrine hormones guanylin and uroguanylin early in colorectal carcinogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Supports GUCY2C as a tumor-suppressive axis silenced early in colorectal carcinogenesis by loss of its endogenous ligands.

steps/1.description: The intestinal receptor guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C) enforces epithelial homeostasis and restrains crypt proliferation. Early in colorectal carcinogenesis its endogenous hormones guanylin and uroguanylin are lost, silencing GUCY2C-cGMP signaling and removing a tumor-suppressive brake — a change that permits progression along the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and is the rationale for GUCY2C-agonist chemoprevention.

evidence.snippet: Molecular studies support the clinical impression that adenocarcinoma of the large intestine develops in stages. At the center of the pathological continuum between normal mucosa and invasive carcinoma is the premalignant lesion, the adenomatous polyp.
evidence.explanation: The abstract describes stage-wise progression through adenomatous polyps.

steps/2.description: Stepwise progression from adenomatous polyps to invasive carcinoma drives colon adenocarcinoma development.

evidence.snippet: Intestinal cancer is initiated by Wnt-pathway-activating mutations in genes such as adenomatous polyposis coli (APC).
evidence.explanation: The abstract identifies APC loss and Wnt pathway activation as initiating events in intestinal cancer.

steps/3.description: Wnt-pathway-activating loss of APC in intestinal stem cells drives early neoplasia.

evidence.snippet: KRAS and BRAF mutations are associated with inferior survival, independent of MSI status, in Japanese patients with curatively resected CRC.
evidence.explanation: This supports the clinical importance of KRAS and BRAF signaling even after accounting for MSI status.

steps/4.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer typically evolves on a background of APC/WNT pathway dysregulation, with KRAS and BRAF alterations shaping invasion, therapy response, and liver metastatic fitness. These pathways reinforce proliferative signaling and resistance to anoikis during dissemination.

evidence.snippet: Metastasis of the liver from colorectal cancer represents the final stage of a multistep biological process.
evidence.explanation: This supports a sequential detachment, invasion, and colonization program in metastatic CRC that is consistent with EMT-linked dissemination.

steps/5.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer cells detach from the primary epithelium, invade through vascular and stromal barriers, and colonize the liver through a stepwise dissemination program consistent with EMT-linked invasive plasticity.

evidence.snippet: MM tumors exhibited suppressed ferroptosis and activation of the TGF-β signaling pathway, while SM tumors displayed inhibited anoikis and activation of the WNT signaling pathway, accompanied by activated angiogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports inhibition of anoikis as a distinct metastatic program in colorectal cancer liver metastasis.

steps/6.description: A subset of metastatic colorectal cancers survives matrix detachment during transit, allowing circulating or portal-disseminating cells to persist long enough to seed the liver and other distant niches.

evidence.snippet: The liver is the first location of metastatic disease; due to that the main mechanism of dissemination is through the portal system.
evidence.explanation: This supports the dominant hepatic tropism of metastatic colorectal cancer.

steps/7.description: The liver is the dominant first metastatic site because colorectal venous drainage enters the portal circulation and because hepatic stromal, endothelial, and immune niches support tumor cell arrest and outgrowth.

evidence.snippet: MM tumors exhibited suppressed ferroptosis and activation of the TGF-β signaling pathway, while SM tumors displayed inhibited anoikis and activation of the WNT signaling pathway, accompanied by activated angiogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports activated angiogenesis as a distinct metastatic CRC program.

steps/8.description: Metastatic colorectal cancer promotes angiogenic remodeling at secondary sites to sustain micrometastatic survival, vascular adaptation, and outgrowth in the hepatic microenvironment.

evidence.snippet: Within the "seed and soil" paradigm, disrupting both tumor cells and their supportive microenvironment is essential to suppress disease progression.
evidence.explanation: This explicitly frames colorectal liver metastasis in seed-and-soil terms.

steps/9.description: Metastatic outgrowth depends on reciprocal signaling between tumor cells and stromal populations such as cancer-associated fibroblasts, which help create a permissive hepatic microenvironment and immunosuppressive niche.

edges/1.description: APC loss establishes the WNT-dysregulated background on which acquired KRAS and BRAF alterations cooperate to shape invasion and therapy response.

edges/2.description: Loss of GUCY2C tumor-suppressive signaling removes a brake on crypt proliferation, permitting adenoma-to-carcinoma progression.

edges/3.description: Cooperating WNT and RAS signalling drives the invasive programs by which tumour cells detach from the primary epithelium and breach stromal barriers.

edges/4.description: Colonising tumour cells engage hepatic stromal populations, including cancer-associated fibroblasts, that create a permissive metastatic niche.

edges/5.description: Hepatic micrometastases drive angiogenic remodelling to sustain vascular adaptation and outgrowth at the secondary site.

edges/6.description: Cells that have detached from the epithelial matrix must survive that detachment to persist during portal transit.

edges/7.description: Detachment-resistant cells persist in the portal circulation long enough to arrest and colonise the liver, the dominant first metastatic site.

genes/0.notes: APC inactivation is the canonical initiator of WNT pathway activation in colorectal carcinogenesis and metastatic progression.

genes/1.notes: KRAS mutations promote metastatic fitness, EGFR resistance, and inferior survival.

genes/2.notes: BRAF, especially V600E, is linked to aggressive metastatic behavior and poor prognosis.

genes/3.notes: MSI-high tumors have distinct immune biology and may respond better to checkpoint blockade despite advanced disease.

evidence.snippet: The colonoscopic study presented a tumor in the ascending colon, which after surgical resection and pathological studies, turned out to be a primary colonoc adenosquamous carcinoma.
evidence.explanation: The abstract describes surgical resection of a colon tumor.

treatments/0.description: Surgical removal of the colon tumor when localized.

evidence.snippet: We performed a randomized, double-blind trial of aspirin as a chemopreventive agent against colorectal adenomas.
evidence.explanation: Establishes aspirin as a randomized-trial-tested chemopreventive agent against colorectal adenomas.

treatments/1.description: Low-dose aspirin is an established chemopreventive ("interception") agent that reduces the recurrence of colorectal adenomas — the precursor lesions of colon adenocarcinoma. The cited randomized trial evaluated secondary prevention in higher-risk individuals with a recent history of documented adenomas; the 81 mg dose reduced adenoma recurrence while 325 mg did not. Its antineoplastic effect in the large bowel is attributed largely to inhibition of COX/prostaglandin-driven pro-tumorigenic signaling within the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Preventive use is balanced against gastrointestinal bleeding risk.

evidence.snippet: Low-dose aspirin has a moderate chemopreventive effect on adenomas in the large bowel.
evidence.explanation: Randomized-trial evidence that low-dose aspirin reduces colorectal adenomas, supporting the INHIBITS edge on the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Aspirin reduces the incidence of colorectal adenomas and advanced neoplasia, intercepting the adenoma-to-carcinoma progression that drives colon adenocarcinoma.

evidence.snippet: The study results highlight the importance of developing a novel GUCY2C agonist formulated for release and activity targeted to the large intestine for colorectal cancer prevention
evidence.explanation: Supports GUCY2C-agonist chemoprevention as a strategy while noting the current formulation is inadequate for the colorectum — an honest limitation.

treatments/2.description: Oral GUCY2C agonists (linaclotide, plecanatide) aim to reactivate the tumor-suppressive GUCY2C axis that is silenced early in colorectal carcinogenesis, restoring cGMP-dependent homeostatic signaling and restraining epithelial proliferation. In a human study oral linaclotide activated GUCY2C and reduced colorectal epithelial proliferation, but only after colon preparation — the FDA-approved gastric-release formulation does not reliably reach the colorectum, so a colorectum-targeted formulation is required before this can serve as a chemopreventive.

evidence.snippet: GUCY2C activation by oral linaclotide was associated with homeostatic signaling, including phosphorylation of vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein and inhibition of proliferation quantified by reduced Ki67-positive epithelial cells.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that a GUCY2C agonist reactivates homeostatic signaling and reduces epithelial proliferation, supporting the RESTORES edge.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: GUCY2C agonists substitute for the lost guanylin/uroguanylin ligands, reactivating GUCY2C-cGMP signaling and restoring the tumor-suppressive brake on crypt proliferation.

evidence.snippet: An immune response was observed only in vaccine recipients.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the MUC1 peptide vaccine is immunogenic in the colorectal adenoma prevention setting.

treatments/3.description: MUC1 is an epithelial glycoprotein aberrantly expressed on colorectal adenomas and carcinomas, making it a candidate shared antigen for immunoprevention. A MUC1 peptide vaccine aims to raise anti-MUC1 immunity to intercept recurrent adenoma formation in individuals with a prior advanced adenoma. In a randomized, placebo-controlled prevention trial the vaccine was immunogenic only in vaccine recipients but did not significantly reduce adenoma recurrence overall; a 38% absolute reduction was seen in the subset who mounted an immune response. It remains investigational.

evidence.snippet: a 38% absolute reduction in adenoma recurrence compared with placebo was observed in participants who had an immune response at week 12 and with the booster injection.
evidence.explanation: Randomized-trial evidence of a hypothesis-generating signal — a 38% absolute reduction in adenoma recurrence was observed only in immune responders and was not statistically significant (P = 0.08), with no effect in the intention-to-treat population (P = 0.25) — supporting a qualified, non-confirmatory INHIBITS edge on the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Anti-MUC1 immunity is intended to eliminate MUC1-overexpressing adenomatous epithelium and reduce adenoma recurrence, intercepting the adenoma-carcinoma sequence; in the trial the vaccine did not reduce adenoma recurrence in the intention-to-treat population (aRR 0.83, 95% CI 0.60-1.14, P = 0.25), and the 38% absolute reduction observed in immune responders was likewise not statistically significant (aRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.15-1.11, P = 0.08) — hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

evidence.snippet: The positive BEACON colorectal cancer (CRC) safety lead-in, evaluating encorafenib + cetuximab + binimetinib in previously treated patients with BRAFV600E-mutated metastatic CRC (mCRC), prompted the design of the phase II ANCHOR CRC study (ClinicalTrails.gov identifier: NCT03693170 ).
evidence.explanation: The phase II ANCHOR CRC study directly evaluates this BRAF/MEK/EGFR targeted combination in BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic CRC.

treatments/4.description: Encorafenib, binimetinib, and cetuximab provide a targeted regimen for BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, pairing BRAF and MEK inhibition with EGFR blockade to suppress MAPK feedback signaling.

evidence.snippet: partial response was achieved in 64 patients with APC-mutated tumors (85%) and 17 patients with APC wild type tumors (59%). There was a significant difference in the objective response rate (ORR) between patients with APC mutation and wild type (p-value of 0.003).
evidence.explanation: This clinical study demonstrates APC mutation status as a predictive biomarker for cetuximab response in RAS wild-type disease, with significantly higher objective response rates in APC-mutant patients.

evidence.snippet: The median OS was not reached (95% CI, 31.5-NA) in patients with the APC mutation, whereas it was 37.3 months (95% CI, 23.4-NA) in those with APC-wild type tumors (p = 0.024).
evidence.explanation: APC-mutant patients treated with cetuximab-containing chemotherapy show significantly longer median overall survival compared to APC wild-type patients.

treatments/5.description: Cetuximab combined with chemotherapy for RAS wild-type metastatic CRC shows improved outcomes in APC-mutant tumors. APC mutation status serves as a predictive biomarker, with APC-mutant tumors achieving higher response rates and longer overall survival compared to APC wild-type tumors, suggesting that Wnt pathway dysregulation influences EGFR inhibitor sensitivity.

evidence.snippet: alcohol (respiratory depression), recreational drugs (varied effects including death), and prescription as well as non-prescription medications/sedatives/anesthetics that could induce respiratory depression
evidence.explanation: Names the agents and the mechanism (respiratory depression) by which they act, which is what distinguishes this arm from the asphyxial one.

evidence.snippet: alcohol (respiratory depression), recreational drugs (varied effects including death)
evidence.explanation: Names alcohol and its mechanism (respiratory depression) in the source's own avoid-list. The quote runs on into recreational drugs because that is where the source's sentence ends; those are curated on the sedative entry above, not here.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Swimming and breath-holding contests (risk of asphyxia, death)
evidence.explanation: Names the circumstances and the stated consequence; the mechanistic reading in the description follows from the absent chemoreflex curated upstream.

evidence.snippet: We found heterozygous de novo mutations in PHOX2B in 18 of 29 individuals with CCHS.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery finding establishing PHOX2B mutation as the cause and its de novo, heterozygous character.

evidence.snippet: Most mutations consisted of 5-9 alanine expansions within a 20-residue polyalanine tract probably resulting from non-homologous recombination.
evidence.explanation: Defines the characteristic mutation class and its likely origin, which is what makes the genotype an interpretable severity predictor.

evidence.snippet: A PHOX2B mutation is required to confirm the diagnosis of CCHS. Knowledge of the specific PHOX2B mutation aids in anticipating the CCHS phenotype severity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the diagnostic requirement and the genotype-phenotype correlation on which clinical anticipation rests.

steps/4.description: The trigger. PHOX2B encodes a paired-like homeobox transcription factor that is a master regulator of visceral reflex circuit development. Heterozygous de novo mutation causes the disorder, and the mutation class is unusual: most are expansions of 5-9 alanines within a normal 20-residue polyalanine tract, probably arising by non-homologous recombination rather than by point mutation. The expansion length predicts phenotype severity closely enough that genotype guides clinical anticipation, which is why testing is diagnostic rather than confirmatory. A minority carry non-polyalanine repeat mutations - frameshift and missense - which produce more severe disease and a higher risk of the neural-crest tumour complications.

evidence.snippet: Neurons of the retrotrapezoïd nucleus/parafacial respiratory group (RTN/pFRG) were found severely depleted in these mice and no other neuronal loss could be identified.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the identity of the lost population and the selectivity of the loss, which is what makes this node a specific lesion rather than a general developmental failure.

evidence.snippet: Physiological experiments show that RTN/pFRG neurons are crucial to driving proper breathing at birth and are necessary for central chemoreception and the generation of a normal respiratory rhythm.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the functional necessity of the lost population, which is what links this node to the chemoreflex failure below it.

evidence.snippet: To date, the reason for the selective vulnerability of RTN/pFRG neurons to PHOX2B protein dysfunction remains unexplained.
evidence.explanation: Cited as PARTIAL because it records the limit of the mechanism rather than supporting it: the selectivity is observed and unexplained, which is the open question named in the node description.

steps/5.description: The mechanistically decisive step, and the reason this disorder is so informative about normal physiology. In mice carrying the commonest CCHS-causing mutation, the retrotrapezoid nucleus / parafacial respiratory group is severely depleted, and NO OTHER neuronal loss can be identified - an extraordinarily selective lesion for a transcription factor expressed throughout the visceral reflex circuitry. Those neurons are necessary for central chemoreception and for generating a normal respiratory rhythm at birth. The selectivity is itself unexplained: why this particular population should be uniquely vulnerable to mutant PHOX2B remains unknown, and it is the central open question of the disorder's cell biology.

evidence.snippet: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS or Ondine's curse; OMIM 209880) is a life-threatening disorder involving an impaired ventilatory response to hypercarbia and hypoxemia.
evidence.explanation: Defines the disorder by exactly the failure this node encodes - an impaired ventilatory response to both chemical stimuli.

evidence.snippet: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is characterized by hypoventilation during sleep and impaired ventilatory responses to hypercapnia and hypoxemia.
evidence.explanation: Independently states the chemoreflex failure and pairs it with its state-dependent expression, which is the link to the node below.

steps/6.description: The central, disorder-defining physiological abnormality: rising arterial carbon dioxide and falling oxygen fail to produce the corrective increase in ventilation that they produce in everyone else. The defect is in the sensing and reflex limb, not in the effector - the lungs, chest wall, and respiratory muscles are normal and can be driven perfectly well, which is why mechanical ventilation works and why the disorder is compatible with normal life expectancy given adequate support. Patients characteristically do not experience dyspnoea during hypoventilation, because the sensation of air hunger depends on the same chemoreceptive input that is missing - a feature that makes the condition dangerous rather than merely limiting.

evidence.snippet: a rare disease defined by the lack of CO(2) responsiveness and of breathing automaticity in sleep
evidence.explanation: States the state dependence explicitly - loss of breathing automaticity specifically in sleep - which is what this node encodes.

evidence.snippet: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is characterized by alveolar hypoventilation and autonomic dysregulation.
evidence.explanation: Pairs the alveolar hypoventilation of this node with the autonomic arm curated separately, which is how the policy statement frames the disorder.

steps/7.description: The state dependence is the disorder's clinical signature and follows directly from how breathing is controlled. Wakefulness supplies a behavioural and cortical drive to breathe that is independent of chemoreception; sleep withdraws it, leaving the automatic chemoreflex loop alone in charge. Where that loop is absent, sleep produces progressive hypoventilation with hypercapnia and hypoxaemia, most severely in non-REM sleep, when chemoreceptive control normally dominates most completely. Severe cases hypoventilate when awake as well. Untreated, the consequence is cor pulmonale, hypoxic neurological injury, and death - the historical natural history that gave the disorder its Ondine's-curse name.

evidence.snippet: This core phenotype is associated with lower-penetrance anomalies of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) including Hirschsprung disease and tumors of neural-crest derivatives such as ganglioneuromas and neuroblastomas.
evidence.explanation: Names the autonomic and neural-crest complications and records their lower penetrance relative to the respiratory core phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We show that PHOX2B is expressed in both the central and the peripheral ANS during human embryonic development.
